note: The discovery document at GET /api/mte-relay. It is the one protocol surface that had no vector, no shared type, and an independent spelling in every implementation, and the rule that no implementation invents a member was held by a comment in one Go file. members is the registered set with the type each name carries; registry.md holds the same names in prose and this file is what a build is measured against. A build that serves or reads a member absent from members has invented one. documents drive every client parser: a parser asserts only the members it consumes, because different carriers need different ones, but it has to agree on the value of every member it does consume.

members.name: discoverySchema
members.note: The shape of this document. A client that does not know the value refuses rather than guessing which members mean what.

members.name: buildVersion
members.note: The full version of the build that answered, not the protocol. Informational: a client keys behavior on features, never on this. The endpoint is unauthenticated, so this publishes the build an operator is running to anyone who asks; that exposure is accepted deliberately in exchange for a version an operator and a support engineer can read without shell access. Absorbed generation and serverVersion, both of which named a piece of what this carries. Named for the binary rather than a product because mte-relay, socketx and tcpq all serve this document and a client is not meant to tell them apart from it; see registry.md.

members.name: frameVersions
members.note: Every frame version this build serves. A client that speaks none of them cannot pair and refuses here.

members.name: deprecatedFrameVersions
members.note: Versions still served but on the way out. Present only once a second version exists, so no build sends it today.

members.name: features
members.note: Registry feature names. This is the only thing a client keys behavior on.

members.name: mteProfile
members.note: The MTE build string. A mismatch means the two libraries cannot pair, whatever else agrees.

members.name: configVersion
members.note: The applied configuration version. Informational.

members.name: kyberStrength
members.note: 512, 768 or 1024. Anything else is a value a client cannot instantiate.

members.name: sequenceWindow
members.note: A pairing input and not a hint. Signed: the relay ships minus 63.

members.name: timeWindow
members.note: A pairing input and not a hint. Both ends construct the decoder with it, so a disagreement is no pair at all rather than a degraded one, and nothing in the failure says why. Zero is a legal MTE window and is also the Go zero value a server sends when the block that fills this member did not run, and the wire cannot tell the two apart, so a client falls back to 1000 rather than adopting it. A server closes the ambiguity at its end by seeding the member with the value it would actually use.

members.name: maxFrameBytes
members.note: The largest single frame the relay will read.

members.name: maxMessageBytes
members.note: The largest reassembled message, across a fragment run.

members.name: maxMetadataBytes
members.note: An object keyed MKE and MTE, uppercase on the wire unlike every other use of the encode type name.

members.name: maxPairsPerBatch
members.note: Batch pairing over HTTP. A carrier that pairs in band sends one pair per connection and has no batch.

members.name: maxPairsPerClient
members.note: Batch pairing over HTTP, and the bound on a keepalive drop list.

members.name: maxPairBytes
members.note: The rekey budget per direction. A client polls its own pair against it.

members.name: maxPairSeconds
members.note: The rekey budget in time.

members.name: maxRequestSeconds
members.note: The request deadline. On a WebSocket it is reused as the run deadline rather than adding a field, which is worth knowing before tuning it.

members.name: maxResponseSeconds
members.note: The response deadline. Zero on a socket, which has no response cycle after the upgrade.

members.name: idleTimeoutSeconds
members.note: How long a connection may be silent.

members.name: pingIntervalSeconds
members.note: How often the relay pings.

members.name: drainSeconds
members.note: How long after a drain signal the relay keeps a connection. It has to be the budget that actually closes the connection, not a wider shutdown budget the connection never sees.

members.name: sessionTimeoutSeconds
members.note: How long stored session state lives. Zero where state dies with the connection.

members.name: tokenMaxAgeSeconds
members.note: How long a client token verifies.

members.name: ownerSeconds
members.note: Owner mode only. No build sends it today.

members.name: transports
members.note: Which carriers this build serves. A relay that serves only one still sends an array.

members.name: wsPath
members.note: Where the WebSocket endpoint lives. Absent from a build that serves none.

members.name: tcpTargets
members.note: TCP alias names only, never host and port. Absent from a build that serves no TCP.

members.name: stateMode
members.note: Informational: how pair state is held.

members.name: routeHeader
members.note: Informational: the header a router keys on.

members.name: maxRequestBodyBytes
members.note: HTTP only. The largest request body the relay proxies.

members.name: passThroughRoutes
members.note: HTTP only. Routes the relay forwards without encoding.

members.name: forwardPlainHeaders
members.note: HTTP only. Headers forwarded outside the ciphertext.

members.name: forwardBrowserCookies
members.note: HTTP only.

documents.name: http_relay
documents.note: An HTTP relay as mte-relay ships it. Carries the HTTP only members and no wsPath.

documents.name: websocket_relay
documents.note: A WebSocket relay as socketx ships it. No batch pairing members, no HTTP forwarding members, and wsPath present.

documents.name: minimal
documents.note: Only the members both servers always send. A parser must not require an optional member in order to read this document.

documents.name: unknown_members
documents.note: A document from a later relay major version. A parser has to ignore members it does not know and read the ones it does, or every future addition breaks every shipped client. This is the forward compatibility the versioning policy rests on.

documents.name: zero_windows
documents.note: The two pairing inputs at zero, which is where they disagree on purpose. A zero timeWindow is not adopted: it is a legal window and also the Go zero value a server sends when the block that fills it did not run, the wire cannot tell those apart, and only one reading is safe. Falling back to 1000 pairs with a server that meant 1000; adopting a spurious zero pairs with nothing and says nothing about why. A zero sequenceWindow is adopted, because every client already adopts any integer there and the default is minus 63, so a zero is the less likely accident. Both servers now seed both members with the values they would use, so neither zero should reach a client from a build in this workspace; this document pins what happens if one does.
